description:
You have power over your mind — not outside events. Realize this, and you will find strength.
 
 Reflection: The only domain you truly govern is how you interpret and respond to what happens to you. Everything else lies outside your sovereignty.
 
 Practice for today: When something goes sideways, pause and ask "Is this mine to control?" If no — exhale and let it pass. If yes — act immediately.

Source quote: "We reacted more strongly to frustrations than normal people." — As Bill Sees It, p. 111
 
 Message: Today's reflection tackles everyday impatience — slow traffic, a restaurant that takes too long. The technique of "levitating" above a frustrating situation to see it from God's perspective reveals that most of our impatience has no real justification. Slow down before God has to slow you down.

"His divine power has given us everything we need for a godly life through our knowledge of him who called us by his own glory and goodness."
 
 Context: Written by Peter around 65–68 AD as he faced execution under Nero. His message to scattered, anxious believers: everything you need is already yours. The gap is not in God's provision — it's in our recognition of what we already hold.

Word: foible (noun) — FOY-bul
 
 Definition: A minor flaw or shortcoming in someone's character or behaviour. In fencing: the weakest part of a sword blade, between the middle and the tip.
 
 Etymology: Borrowed from French in the 1600s. Originally referred to the weak portion of a fencing blade. Traces back to Old French "feble" — also the ancestor of "feeble." Crossed from swordsmanship vocabulary into character description by the late 17th century, softening from "dangerous weakness" to "endearing minor flaw."

Alcoholics Anonymous is founded. In Akron, Ohio, Bill Wilson and Dr. Robert Smith ("Dr. Bob") had their first meeting and Dr. Bob took his last drink. AA's peer-support model — two alcoholics simply talking about shared experience — has since influenced addiction treatment and mental health programs worldwide. Today is AA's 91st birthday.

First execution of the Salem witch trials. Bridget Bishop was hanged at Gallows Hill in Massachusetts. Her colorful dress and outspoken personality made her an easy target in the hysteria that claimed 19 lives before the special court was dissolved. A defining case study in mass hysteria and accusation without evidence.

Benjamin Franklin flies a kite in a thunderstorm. Franklin collected electrical charge in a Leyden jar, demonstrating the link between lightning and electricity. This directly led to the invention of the lightning rod. Franklin never published a firsthand account, leading some historians to question the precise details.

Wagner's Tristan und Isolde premieres in Munich. Its opening chord — the "Tristan chord" — is one of the most analyzed moments in Western music history, marking the beginning of the breakdown of traditional tonality. It directly influenced Debussy, Mahler, and the 20th-century modernist movement.

Italy declares war on France and Britain. With German forces occupying Paris, Mussolini declared war — described by FDR as "the hand that held the dagger struck it into the back of its neighbour." Italy's entry was largely opportunistic; the military was widely unprepared for what followed.

The Six-Day War ends. Israel and Syria agreed to a UN-mediated ceasefire ending six days of fighting that also involved Egypt and Jordan. Israel captured the Sinai Peninsula, Gaza Strip, West Bank, East Jerusalem, and Golan Heights — reshaping the Middle East in ways still felt today.

The Village That Refused to Be Rebuilt — Oradour-sur-Glane.
 
 In June 1944, Nazi Waffen-SS troops massacred 642 men, women, and children in this French village, burning the church with women and children locked inside. After the war, President de Gaulle ordered the village NOT rebuilt — preserved exactly as the SS left it (roofless walls, burned-out cars, children's shoes still on floors) as a permanent open-air memorial. A new village was built nearby. De Gaulle's reasoning: the ruins speak more powerfully than any monument could.

source: A · Marcus Aurelius - Meditations — Stoic Reflection
description:
"You have power over your mind, not outside events. Realize this, and you will find strength."

Reflection: Marcus wrote this amid empire, plague, and betrayal. He reminds us that we cannot control whether Secor audits pile up or Bathrooms need scrubbing twice — but we CAN choose how we meet the day.

Today's Practice: When something frustrates you, pause and ask: Is this in my control? If not, release it. If yes, act.

source: B · AA Daily Reflection - FAMILY OBLIGATIONS — AA p. 129
description:
Title: FAMILY OBLIGATIONS

"...a spiritual life which does not include...family obligations may not be so perfect after all."

Message: We can be doing well in all public areas of our lives and still find that things at home have quietly unraveled. Progress in recovery — and in life — must show up in how we treat the people closest to us. Patience, real amends, and genuine presence matter more than grand gestures. "The spiritual life is not a theory. We have to live it."

"May the favor of the Lord our God rest on us; establish the work of our hands for us — yes, establish the work of our hands."
— Psalm 90:17 (NIV)

Context: This is Moses' prayer — the only Psalm attributed to him — written after Israel's long desert wandering. Moses understood fragile, transient effort. He asked God not just for blessing but for lasting fruit. A powerful anchor on a task-heavy day.

source: D · Word of the Day - Merriam-Webster — foible (FOY-bul)
description:
Word: FOIBLE  [FOY-bul]  noun

Definition: A minor flaw or weakness in someone's character or behavior.

Example: "You have to be able to laugh at your own foibles."

Etymology: From French via Old French 'feble' (also the root of 'feeble'). Originally the weakest part of a fencing sword — between the middle and the tip. By the 1600s it crossed over to describe minor failings of character.

Fun fact: Even the word for weakness has a weak spot — its root literally means feeble.

source: E · This Day in History - June 11 — Key Events
description:
• 323 BC — Alexander the Great died at age 32 in Babylon, ending one of history's most astonishing empires.
• 1509 — Henry VIII married Catherine of Aragon — setting in motion events that would break England from Rome and reshape Western Christianity.
• 1776 — Continental Congress formed the 'Committee of Five' (Jefferson, Adams, Franklin, Sherman, Livingston) to draft a Declaration of Independence.
• 1919 — Sir Barton won the Belmont Stakes, becoming the first Triple Crown winner in US racing history.
• 1959 — Christopher Cockerell publicly demonstrated the first hovercraft (SR.N1).
• 1977 — Seattle Slew won the Triple Crown.
• 2010 — FIFA World Cup opened in South Africa — the first time the African continent hosted the tournament.

source: F · Britannica Fact - Surprising Encyclopaedia Fact
description: Alexander the Great — who died June 11, 323 BC — had a condition called heterochromia: one eye was blue and one was brown. His horse Bucephalus was said to be so wild that only Alexander could ride him, reportedly because Alexander noticed the horse was simply afraid of its own shadow and turned it to face the sun. The horse died in battle in 326 BC and Alexander founded a city (Bucephala, in present-day Pakistan) in his honor. A conqueror naming a city after his horse — that's the kind of detail history books usually skip.

source: A · Marcus Aurelius Meditations — Book IV
description:
"Loss is nothing else but change, and change is Nature's delight."

Reflection: Marcus wrote this while ruling an empire in constant flux — wars, plagues, political shifts. He trained himself to see every ending as transformation, not destruction. The Carnival is starting today in Bruderheim. The Secor Audit rolled over from yesterday. Things shift. That's the nature of days.

Application: What if today's rescheduled items aren't failures — but the day rearranging itself into what it actually needs to be?

Practice for today: When something doesn't go to plan, say inwardly: 'Change is nature's delight.' Then act.

source: B · AA Daily Reflection FORMING TRUE PARTNERSHIPS — 12 & 12 p.53
description:
Title: FORMING TRUE PARTNERSHIPS

From the 12 & 12: The core insight is that our most persistent suffering comes not from dramatic crises but from our broken relationships — with family, friends, the world around us. The real problem is recognizing our tendency to withhold full, honest partnership from others.

Message: Recovery (and a good life) isn't a solo project. It requires real connection — not performance or people-pleasing, but genuine openness to being known and knowing others. Today, with 1:1s with Logan and Oliver on the calendar, this is practical: show up actually present, not just physically there.

"Who is going to harm you if you are eager to do good?"
— 1 Peter 3:13 (NIV)

Also: YouVersion today — "Love is patient and kind; love does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant." — 1 Corinthians 13:4

Context: Peter wrote to scattered, persecuted Christians who feared for their safety. His reassurance wasn't naïve — it was a call to keep doing good regardless of circumstance. The person eager to do good is not unprotected; they are sustained by purpose itself.

Reflection: On a day with rescheduled audits and carry-over tasks, the question 'who will harm you?' reframes anxiety. What harm can pile-up truly do to someone who keeps moving forward?

source: D · Word of the Day Merriam-Webster — blandishment (BLAN-dish-munt)
description:
Word: BLANDISHMENT  [BLAN-dish-munt]  noun (usually plural)

Definition: Words or actions that flatter and coax — designed to persuade or win over through charm rather than logic.

Example: "He sought to turn the attack around by saying his vast wealth made him immune to the blandishments of plutocrats."

Etymology: From French 'blandir' (to flatter), rooted in Latin 'blandus' (mild, flattering). The -ment suffix makes it a noun of action or result. It shares roots with 'bland' — originally meaning soft or agreeable, not the 'boring' sense we use today.

Fun connection: When Star Wars' Lando Calrissian offered Cloud City hospitality to Han and Leia, that was pure blandishment — charm concealing a trap.

source: E · This Day in History June 12 — Key Events Across History
description:
• 1665 — England installs a municipal government in New York, previously the Dutch settlement of New Amsterdam. The city's Dutch roots (Brooklyn = Breuckelen, Harlem = Haarlem) survive to this day.
• 1776 — Virginia's colonial legislature becomes the first to adopt a Bill of Rights, establishing the template for the US Constitution's first ten amendments.
• 1898 — The Philippines declares independence from Spain after 300 years of colonial rule, during the Spanish-American War. Independence would prove short-lived as the US annexed the Philippines in the peace treaty.
• 1939 — The National Baseball Hall of Fame and Museum is dedicated in Cooperstown, NY.
• 1942 — Anne Frank, 13, receives a diary for her birthday in Amsterdam. Less than a month later, she and her family go into hiding from the Nazis.
• 1963 — Civil rights leader Medgar Evers, 37, is shot and killed outside his home in Jackson, Mississippi.
• 1964 — Nelson Mandela is sentenced to life in prison for sabotage against apartheid. He would serve 27 years before his release in 1990.
• 1967 — The US Supreme Court unanimously strikes down laws banning interracial marriage in Loving v. Virginia — now celebrated as National Loving Day.
• 1987 — President Reagan, at the Brandenburg Gate: 'Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!'
• 1994 — Boeing's 777 goes on its first test flight.

source: F · Britannica Fact Surprising Fact for June 12
description: Anne Frank received her diary on this date in 1942 — but most people don't know that she actually rewrote the entire diary herself. After hearing a 1944 Dutch radio broadcast encouraging people to keep records of life under occupation, Anne went back through her entries and deliberately revised and edited them, intending to publish the diary as a novel after the war. The version her father Otto published in 1947 was a composite of both her original entries and her own edited revisions. Anne was not just a witness — she was an intentional author who understood she was writing for an audience. She was 15 when she began her revisions. She died at Bergen-Belsen in February or March 1945, aged 15.

"Waste no more time arguing what a good person should be. Be one."

Reflection: Marcus cuts through overthinking. Character is built in repeated ordinary choices — how we answer stress, how we speak to our kids, how we handle unfinished work.

Practice for today: Choose one small concrete act of goodness and do it immediately without announcing it.

"And acceptance is the answer to all my problems today."

Message: Fighting reality drains energy that could be used to move forward. Acceptance is not approval — it is seeing clearly enough to take the next right action.

"Let us not become weary in doing good, for at the proper time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up."

Context: Paul encouraged exhausted believers to continue faithfully even when results were slow. Consistency matters more than intensity.

source: D · Word of the Day — steadfast
description:
Definition: Firmly loyal, unwavering, dependable.

Example: 'She remained steadfast even when the schedule changed around her.'

• 1966 — The U.S. Supreme Court issued the Miranda decision requiring police to inform suspects of their rights.
• 1983 — Pioneer 10 became the first spacecraft to leave the central solar system region.
Octopuses have three hearts and blue blood. Two hearts move blood to the gills while the third circulates it through the body.

"The happiness of your life depends upon the quality of your thoughts."

Reflection: Attention shapes experience. The stories we repeat internally become the atmosphere we live in.

Practice for today: Replace one recurring negative thought with a deliberate truthful one.
Growth often happens slowly and quietly. Patience with ourselves and others creates room for healing that force never can.

"Trust in the Lord with all your heart and lean not on your own understanding."

Reflection: Trust does not remove uncertainty — it gives us courage to continue through it.

source: D · Word of the Day — luminous
description:
Definition: Giving off light; intellectually inspiring or clear.

Example: 'Her explanation was so luminous that everyone understood immediately.'

• 1777 — The Continental Congress adopted the Stars and Stripes as the flag of the United States.
• 1967 — Mariner 5 launched toward Venus to study the planet's atmosphere.
Venus rotates so slowly and in the opposite direction of most planets that a day on Venus is longer than its year.

"The impediment to action advances action. What stands in the way becomes the way."

Reflection: Marcus reminds us that obstacles are not interruptions to the path — they become the path. A delay, a difficult task, or a messy morning can be used as training instead of treated as failure.

Practice for today: Pick one thing you are avoiding and turn it into the next small step.

source: B · AA Daily Reflection — Humility and Help
description:
Message: Progress becomes possible when we stop trying to manage everything alone. Humility is not thinking less of yourself; it is being honest enough to accept help, direction, and correction.

Practice for today: Ask for help with one thing before resentment builds.

"Those who hope in the Lord will renew their strength."

Reflection: This verse is about endurance, not instant rescue. Renewal can look like steady breath, a quieter mind, or enough strength for the next faithful action.

source: D · Word of the Day — diligent
description:
Definition: Careful, steady, and persistent in effort.

Example: 'A diligent person does the next right thing even when no one is watching.'

Reflection: Diligence is not perfection. It is returning to the work, again and again.

source: E · This Day in History — June 15
description:
• 1215 — King John sealed Magna Carta at Runnymede, limiting royal power and influencing later constitutional law.
• 1846 — The Oregon Treaty set the 49th parallel as much of the U.S.–Canada border west of the Rockies.
• 1877 — Henry Ossian Flipper became the first Black graduate of West Point.
• 1991 — Mount Pinatubo erupted in the Philippines, one of the largest volcanic eruptions of the 20th century.

Magna Carta was originally a practical peace agreement between King John and rebellious barons, not a modern bill of rights. Its long-term power came from later generations reusing it as a symbol that rulers are also under the law.
\You have power over your mind

Today's reflection, titled "Living Our Amends," draws from the recognition that years spent alongside active addiction leave lasting marks on everyone in the household â€” not just the person drinking. The core message is that making amends is not a single conversation or apology but a daily commitment to showing up differently: sober, present, and consistent. For anyone in recovery or loving someone in recovery, the takeaway is quietly powerful â€” the most eloquent amends is a life visibly changed, one steady day at a time.

source: C Â· Bible Verse of the Day
description: Luke 6:33 (NIV): "And if you do good to those who are good to you, what credit is that to you? Even sinners do that." This verse comes from Jesus's Sermon on the Plain, where he pushes his listeners past the comfortable limits of ordinary reciprocity â€” pointing out that kindness exchanged among friends requires no faith at all. The real measure of character, he argues, is how we treat those who offer us nothing in return.

description: hale (/hayl/) Â· adjective Â· Free from defect, disease, or infirmity; healthy and robust â€” most familiar in the phrase "hale and hearty." Example: Despite being well into his eighties, he remained hale and hearty, walking several miles through the hills each morning. Etymology: From Old English hal, meaning "whole, uninjured, healthy" â€” the same root that gave us "whole," "heal," and "holy," reflecting an ancient understanding that health, completeness, and holiness were all expressions of the same unbroken state.

source: E Â· This Day in History
description: 1777 â€” The 19-year-old Marquis de Lafayette arrived in America, bringing French military expertise that proved critical to the Revolution. | 1966 â€” Miranda v. Arizona established that suspects must be informed of their rights to remain silent and to an attorney. | 1967 â€” President Johnson nominated Thurgood Marshall as the first African American Supreme Court Justice. | 1971 â€” The New York Times began publishing the Pentagon Papers, exposing government deception about the Vietnam War. | 1983 â€” Pioneer 10 became the first human-made object to cross beyond Neptune's orbit. | 2000 â€” The leaders of North and South Korea met face to face for the first time since the Korean War.

When Pioneer 10 crossed beyond Neptune's orbit in 1983, it had been traveling for only eleven years â€” yet it was already leaving the neighborhood of every planet humanity had ever known, carrying a gold-anodized plaque designed to introduce our species to any intelligence that might find it drifting through interstellar space. The spacecraft was built with 1960s technology, weighed less than 260 kilograms, and is still detectable by radio today, now more than 130 astronomical units from the Sun. It is a reminder that the ambition of a civilization is not always proportional to the sophistication of its tools.

Flag Day. "You have power over your mind â€” not outside events. Realize this, and you will find strength." Marcus wrote from the field, governing an empire while burying children and fighting plague, yet insisting that the inner citadel â€” one's judgment â€” could never be stormed by fortune. On a summer Sunday, spend five quiet minutes naming one thing you cannot control today and consciously releasing it. Practice for today: notice the moment you reach for an outcome you cannot dictate, and redirect that energy toward how you will show up instead.

Today's reflection, "When the Going Gets Rough," centers on the idea that the AA program is not a fair-weather tool but a full design for living that holds up when everything falls apart at once. The writer describes early sobriety when job loss, serious illness, and heartbreak all arrived together â€” and found that the habits built in recovery were precisely the anchors needed in the storm. The takeaway: you do not have to wait for calm waters to trust the program. You trust it especially when the waters are rough.

source: C Â· Bible Verse of the Day
description: 1 Samuel 2:7 (NIV): "The Lord sends poverty and wealth; he humbles and he exalts." This verse comes from Hannah's prayer of gratitude after she brought her son Samuel to the tabernacle, having prayed for him through years of barrenness â€” making her declaration of God's sovereignty deeply personal and hard-won. It calls the reader away from pride in good seasons and despair in bad ones, as both are held in a larger hand.

source: D Â· Word of the Day
description: Emblazon (im-BLAY-zun) Â· verb Â· To inscribe or display something prominently on a surface, or to celebrate something conspicuously. Example: Her favorite souvenir from the Grand Canyon was a t-shirt emblazoned with a rosy sunset over the famous chasm. Etymology: From the Anglo-French blason meaning shield; the prefix em- intensifies the base verb, and over time the word shed its strictly heraldic meaning to cover any bold, prominent display.

source: E Â· This Day in History
description: 1775 â€” The Continental Congress authorized the first enlistment of expert riflemen, founding the United States Army. | 1777 â€” The Stars and Stripes officially adopted as the U.S. national flag â€” Flag Day. | 1789 â€” Captain William Bligh reached Timor after a 3,600-mile open-ocean voyage, 47 days after being cast adrift from the Bounty. | 1940 â€” German troops occupied Paris; Auschwitz received its first 728 prisoners on the same day. | 1954 â€” Eisenhower added "under God" to the Pledge of Allegiance. | 1982 â€” British forces captured Stanley, ending the 74-day Falklands War.

When Captain William Bligh was cast adrift in the South Pacific in 1789 with no charts and a 23-foot open boat, he navigated nearly 3,600 miles using dead reckoning alone and lost only one man to violence, not the sea. His handwritten log of that voyage was so accurate it was later used as a navigational reference for the region. It is a reminder that human competence under extreme duress can be more reliable than any instrument.

Magna Carta Day. "You have power over your mind â€” not outside events. Realize this, and you will find strength." On a Monday in mid-June, when the week stretches ahead full of unknowns, apply this anchor by pausing before the first frustration of the morning and asking: Is this within my control? Then release what is not. Practice for today: choose one worry you have been carrying and consciously set it down, returning your energy to what you can actually act on.

Today's reflection, "Making A.A. Your Higher Power," speaks gently to anyone who has felt blocked by the God question in recovery. The message is freeing: you do not need a fully formed faith to begin â€” a table, a tree, or simply the group itself can serve as something greater than yourself to lean on. What matters is willingness, not certainty, and genuine faith tends to arrive quietly on its own, long after we stop demanding it on our terms.

source: C Â· Bible Verse of the Day
description: 1 Peter 2:21 (NIV): "To this you were called, because Christ suffered for you, leaving you an example, that you should follow in his steps." Peter wrote this to early Christians enduring persecution under Roman rule, urging them to respond to unjust hardship with patience rather than retaliation. The verse reminds believers that endurance in difficulty is not weakness but a participation in something redemptive and purposeful.

source: D Â· Word of the Day
description: tenuous (TEN-yoo-us) Â· adjective Â· Having little substance, strength, or certainty; flimsy or weak. Example: "It's an extremely tenuous link to more human interaction" (Jennifer Pattinson Tuohy, The Verge, 2026). Etymology: From Latin tenuis, meaning fine-drawn, thin, or slight â€” a root shared with the English word thin, always carrying that sense of something stretched so fine it might snap.

source: E Â· This Day in History
description: 1215 â€” Magna Carta signed, first placing legal limits on royal power and seeding centuries of constitutional governance. | 1775 â€” George Washington appointed commander-in-chief of the Continental Army. | 1836 â€” Arkansas admitted to the Union as the 25th state. | 1864 â€” Arlington National Cemetery established. | 1904 â€” PS General Slocum fire killed over 1,000 people â€” New York's deadliest event until 9/11. | 1938 â€” Johnny Vander Meer threw his second consecutive no-hitter, a feat never repeated in MLB history.

The Magna Carta of 1215 was not originally intended as a timeless charter of liberty â€” it was a practical peace deal between a desperate king and rebellious barons, and it was annulled by Pope Innocent III within months of being signed. Nearly everything we associate with it as a founding document of human rights was layered on by later generations who needed a precedent to cite. History's most influential guarantees of freedom are often accidental, rescued from obscurity by people who found in them exactly what they needed to believe.

Valentina Tereshkova Day. "You have power over your mind, not outside events. Realize this, and you will find strength." His point was not passivity but sovereignty: external events will arrive unbidden, but the interpretation you give them is entirely yours to author. On a Tuesday in mid-June, when Monday's intentions have faded into the grind, reclaim that inner authority. Practice for today: when something irritates or disappoints you before noon, pause for one full breath and consciously choose your interpretation before you react.

Today's reflection, "Open-Mindedness," carries a quietly radical message: the spiritual path in recovery is not a narrow gate reserved for those with perfect belief or tidy theology â€” it is broad, welcoming, and asks only that you seek honestly. You do not have to have it figured out. The invitation is simply to stay curious, stay humble, and let a little light through the door â€” and that willingness, however small, is itself the beginning of something real.

source: C Â· Bible Verse of the Day
description: John 15:18 (NIV): "If the world hates you, keep in mind that it hated me first." Jesus spoke these words during his final night with his disciples, preparing them for the friction that comes with standing apart from surrounding cultural values. The comfort offered is not exemption from hardship but solidarity â€” rejection, when it comes for doing what is right, is not evidence that something has gone wrong, but that something is going very right.

source: D Â· Word of the Day
description: Gamut (GAM-ut) Â· noun Â· The complete range or extent of something, from one extreme to the other â€” as in "she experienced the full gamut of emotions in a single afternoon." In music, the word once referred to the entire recognized scale of medieval notes. Etymology: From Medieval Latin "gamma ut," combining the Greek letter gamma (assigned to the lowest musical note) with ut, the opening syllable of a Latin hymn; entered English around the 1520s and expanded from music to any complete spectrum.

source: E Â· This Day in History
description: 1775 â€” George Washington appointed Commander in Chief, uniting the colonies behind a single military leader. | 1858 â€” Lincoln's "House Divided" speech warned a nation half slave and half free could not stand. | 1903 â€” Ford Motor Company incorporated in Detroit, launching the industrial era. | 1933 â€” FDR signed Glass-Steagall, creating the FDIC and separating commercial from investment banking. | 1963 â€” Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space, orbiting Earth 48 times. | 1976 â€” The Soweto Uprising: South African police opened fire on student protesters, galvanizing worldwide opposition to apartheid.

When Valentina Tereshkova orbited Earth 48 times in June 1963, she logged more time in space on that single mission than all American astronauts combined had flown up to that point â€” yet the United States would not send a woman to space for another two decades. The gap is a striking reminder that "firsts" in history are rarely followed by swift momentum; breakthroughs often arrive before the culture or institutions are ready to sustain them. Progress moves less like a river and more like a tide â€” advancing in surges, retreating, and advancing again.

Watergate Day. "You have power over your mind, not outside events. Realize this, and you will find strength." Marcus wrote as a Roman emperor who faced constant external pressure â€” military campaigns, loss of children â€” yet returned each morning to the discipline of inner governance. On this Wednesday in mid-June, pause before reacting to any email, frustration, or piece of news, and ask whether your response is chosen or merely reflexive. Practice for today: before your first difficult conversation, take one slow breath and name what you actually control in the situation.

Today's reflection, "Deep Down Within Us," draws from the Big Book's reminder that the most reliable source of strength is not found in external circumstances but in the quiet interior of one's own life. Healing came not from dramatic moments but from the patient, daily practice of showing up â€” to meetings, to the Steps, to honest self-examination â€” until something inside gradually shifted. The invitation today: slow down, do the next small thing, and trust that what you are searching for is already present within you, waiting to be met.

source: C Â· Bible Verse of the Day
description: Psalm 34:6 (NIV): "This poor man called, and the Lord heard him; he saved him out of all his troubles." Psalm 34 was written by David after he survived a perilous situation by feigning madness before a foreign king. The word "poor" here carries a meaning wider than financial â€” it describes a posture of the heart, the person who has run out of self-sufficiency and simply calls out, and finds that the call was heard.

source: D Â· Word of the Day
description: wifty (WIF-tee) Â· adjective Â· Silly, scatterbrained, or charmingly eccentric in a way that suggests the mind has drifted somewhere amusing and unreachable. Example: "She gave a wifty little wave and wandered off toward the garden, having completely forgotten what she came outside to do." Etymology: American English slang of uncertain origin, first surfacing in the mid-20th century â€” belonging to a family of playful adjectives (ditzy, flighty, daffy) that describe minds floating slightly above the practical world.

source: E Â· This Day in History
description: 1775 â€” Battle of Bunker Hill proved untrained militias could stand against a professional army, transforming the Revolution into a serious war. | 1856 â€” First Republican National Convention met in Philadelphia, nominating John C. Fremont. | 1885 â€” The Statue of Liberty arrived in New York in 214 crates; assembled and dedicated the following year. | 1928 â€” Amelia Earhart became the first woman to make the transatlantic flight. | 1972 â€” Watergate break-in: five operatives linked to the Nixon White House arrested at the DNC headquarters, setting in motion the scandal that ended a presidency.

When the Statue of Liberty arrived in New York Harbor on June 17, 1885, she came in 214 crates and sat in storage for over a year while fundraising for her pedestal slowly inched forward, largely through small donations from ordinary Americans. The fact that one of history's most iconic symbols of freedom spent months in a warehouse waiting on crowd-sourced financing is quietly humanizing: even monuments to grand ideals are built incrementally, one modest contribution at a time. The Statue of Liberty was also, for a while, just a pile of copper in crates.

Sally Ride Day. "You have power over your mind â€” not outside events. Realize this, and you will find strength." For a Thursday in mid-June, when the week's momentum can pull you toward reaction rather than intention, this is a grounding anchor. Before responding to any friction today, pause and ask whether your discomfort lives in the event or in your interpretation of it. Practice for today: identify one thing beyond your control that is taking up mental space, name it aloud, and consciously release it.

Today's reflection, "A Fellowship of Freedom," centers on one of AA's quietest miracles: nobody is commanded to do anything. The Steps are suggested, sponsors guide rather than dictate, and meetings run on willing participation â€” yet people keep showing up. The program works precisely because it is chosen, not coerced. A good question to carry today: what am I doing freely now that I once had no say in?

source: C Â· Bible Verse of the Day
description: Jeremiah 31:25 (NIV): "I will refresh the weary and satisfy the faint." This promise comes from Jeremiah 31, known as the Book of Consolation, written during one of Israel's darkest periods of exile and national collapse. God speaks in the first person â€” not through a prophet's paraphrase but directly â€” pledging a deep replenishment of the soul, making it an enduring word for seasons of exhaustion, grief, or spiritual dryness.

source: D Â· Word of the Day

Juneteenth. "You have power over your mind, not outside events. Realize this, and you will find strength." Marcus ruled one of the largest empires in history yet spent his nights writing journal entries about humility. For this Friday, identify one thing you cannot control that is draining your energy, write it down, and consciously set it aside. Practice for today: before you react to anything frustrating, pause for one breath and ask whether the thing causing irritation is truly within your power to change.

description: Romans 12:18 (NIV): "If it is possible, as far as it depends on you, live at peace with everyone." Paul wrote this to a community of believers navigating real social tensions in imperial Rome. The qualifier "as far as it depends on you" is theologically significant: Paul is honest that peace is not always achievable, but places the responsibility for effort squarely on the individual, teaching that peacemaking is an active posture, not a passive hope.

The Emancipation Proclamation was issued in January 1863, yet enslaved people in Texas did not learn of their freedom until June 19, 1865 â€” a full two and a half years later â€” because federal enforcement was simply absent from the region until Union troops physically arrived. This gap between a law existing on paper and that law having any real effect on human lives is one of history's starkest reminders that rights without enforcement are, in practice, no rights at all. Juneteenth is therefore not just a celebration of freedom declared but of freedom actually delivered.
